transcript.content: Hello, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. [Name], it's... it's a lot, really. I mean, the short version is that I came in because I can’t seem to stop launching projects. But it's not just, you know, one or two things. It's everything, all at once. I’m a systems manager, right? So my brain is always looking for ways to optimize, to build, to connect. But lately, it’s just in overdrive. I’ll sit down to check an email, and suddenly I’m drafting three new comprehensive work plans for my department, and then I realize I need to update my certifications, so I map out a whole study schedule for that. 

And then I get home, and I can't just relax. I look at the home network and think, "I can make this faster, more secure," so I'm tearing into the router configurations, running new cables, the whole nine yards. And while I'm doing that, I'm firing off messages to old contacts on LinkedIn, people I haven't spoken to in years, pitching them these grand ideas for tech startups or collaborations. 

It just builds and builds, and it gets so intense that I completely blow past normal limits. I forget to eat, I don't sleep, I just keep going until I hit a wall. And usually, I don't even realize I'm doing it until my wife, Sarah, has to practically pull the keyboard away from me, or my director at work has to pull me into a meeting and tell me to slow down because I'm overwhelming the whole team. It's like I have this engine inside me that's revving at ten thousand RPMs and someone cut the brake lines, you know?
Have you been using any stimulants, recreational drugs, excessive caffeine, or new medications/supplements around the time these episodes of high energy started?

No, no, I know exactly why you're asking that, because it totally sounds like I'm wired on something, right? But honestly, no. I mean, sure, I drink coffee, but just my normal amount. I have this one specific mug, it's insulated, keeps it at exactly the right temperature, and I have one of those in the morning when I get to the office, maybe a second one around two in the afternoon if we're dealing with a server migration or something tedious. But I'm not chugging energy drinks or taking caffeine pills or anything like that. 

As for recreational drugs, absolutely not. I mean, in my line of work, you need a clear head. If I make a mistake configuring a firewall because I'm high on something, that's my job on the line, and I take my career very, very seriously. I've been at the same company for six years, worked my way up to systems manager, and I didn't do that by messing around with drugs. And medications... no, nothing new. I take a multivitamin, you know, the standard kind you get at the pharmacy, just because Sarah read somewhere that it's good for cognitive longevity, but I've been taking those for years. No new supplements, no weird herbal things, nothing like that. It's just... it's just my brain doing this all on its own, which is honestly the most frustrating part, because if it was just too much espresso, I could just stop drinking espresso, you know? But this is just me.
How long has this current stretch of high energy, reduced need for sleep, and non-stop project launching lasted continuously—days, or weeks?

Well, this current stretch... I mean, it's hard to put an exact start and stop date on a specific "stretch," because it feels more like a cycle I've been stuck in for a while now. But if we're talking about this whole pattern—the being unusually driven, the needing barely any sleep, the feeling like I can take on the world and completely reorganize the entire IT infrastructure by myself... that whole overconfident, non-stop project launching thing? It's been going on for roughly a year and eight months. 

I remember because it started right around the time we did the big Q3 server overhaul the year before last. I thought I was just really pumped about the project, you know? I was working late, coming in early, and I felt fantastic. I thought, "Wow, I've finally hit my stride as a manager." But then the project ended, and the energy didn't. I just kept finding new things to overhaul. And Sarah, my wife, she started noticing it then, too. She'd say, "The server migration is done, why are you up at 3 AM mapping out a new disaster recovery protocol?" And I'd just tell her it was necessary, that I was just being proactive. But it's been like that, on and off, but mostly on, for about twenty months now. It's exhausting, but at the same time, when I'm in it, I don't feel exhausted at all. I feel like I'm the only one who can see how everything connects.

Aside from these high-energy stretches, have you ever gone through a separate period—lasting at least a couple of weeks—where you felt persistently down, low on energy, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

Yeah, I... I definitely have. It’s like the pendulum swings completely in the other direction, you know? And it’s not just a day or two of feeling tired after pushing myself too hard. It’s these long, drawn-out periods, easily lasting weeks, sometimes longer, where the engine just completely dies. 

I’ll wake up, and instead of having a million ideas, I just feel like this... this failed version of myself. It’s a physical sensation, almost, just this heavy, flat feeling that pins me to the mattress. I’ll lie there and look at the ceiling, and the thought of getting up, of logging in, of looking at a single line of code or a network map... it makes me feel sick. The things I usually love, the problem-solving, the optimizing—it all seems completely pointless. 

And it’s not just work. It bleeds into everything. Sarah will come in and ask me something totally normal, like what I want for breakfast or if I remembered to pay the water bill, and even just processing the question, formulating an answer... it feels like it takes more energy than I have in my entire body. I’ll just kind of grunt or stare at her, and I know it hurts her feelings, and I feel terribly guilty about it, which just makes the heaviness worse. I’ll sit on the couch for hours, not really watching TV, not really reading, just existing in this gray zone where I have zero motivation and zero interest in anything that normally brings me joy. It’s the exact opposite of the high-energy phases, and honestly, it’s terrifying because when I’m in it, I can’t remember what it feels like to be happy or driven. I just feel broken.

During your most intense high-energy periods, has it ever gotten so extreme that you were hospitalized, lost a job, made major financial decisions you regretted, or experienced things like hearing or seeing things that weren't there?

Well, I've never been hospitalized, and I still have my job, thankfully, though I've definitely had some close calls with HR because of how intense I can get during those stretches. And I haven't gone out and bought a sports car or drained our savings account or anything like that. But... well, things did get really, really strange, and I guess extreme in a different way. 

It was during one of those most driven stretches, you know? When I was barely sleeping, maybe two hours a night, and I was pushing these huge, massive plans to restructure our entire cloud architecture. I was in the server room a lot, which is this incredibly loud, humming environment, right? It's just constant, white noise from the cooling fans. But I started... I started hearing things in the noise. Not just the hum, but actual voices, like comments being made about me. It sounded like people whispering just under the frequency of the fans, critiquing my work, saying I was missing something, or that I was being watched by corporate. I'd stop and hold my breath to listen, and it would fade back into just the fan noise, but the second I started working again, the whispering would start up. 

And then it bled over into my emails and Slack messages. I'd be reading a totally standard message from a vendor or a colleague—something like, "Let's review the deployment schedule on Tuesday"—and I would read these hidden threats into it. I was convinced they were speaking in code, that "Tuesday" was a signal that they were going to try and force me out of my position, or that they had found a flaw in my code and were secretly building a case against me. I'd spend hours, literally hours, analyzing the phrasing of a three-word email, trying to decode the real message. I even started confronting people about it, very cryptically, which is why HR got involved. So, no hospital, no bankruptcy, but... yeah, my mind was definitely playing some terrifying tricks on me, making me see and hear things that, looking back, I know weren't really there. But in the moment, I swear to you, it felt as real as you sitting across from me right now.

Have you ever experienced that whispering or hearing hidden messages in emails during your low, depressed periods or when you're feeling like your normal self, or does it only happen during those high-energy stretches?

Well, that's the thing, and it's something I've spent a lot of time trying to map out in my own head, because you'd think it would just be tied to the lack of sleep and the overdrive, right? Like, the brain is just misfiring from running too hot. But... no, it's not just then. 

I've had periods—several of them, actually—where my mood was completely flat. Not depressed, not lying in bed unable to move, but not energized either. Just... normal, I guess? Or as close to normal as I get. Just calm, going through the motions, sleeping eight hours, eating regular meals. And even during those stretches, which have lasted a few weeks at a time, I've still experienced it. 

I remember one specific time, it was maybe a month after HR talked to me, and I was really making an effort to just lay low and do my job. I felt fine. But I'd look at the Microsoft Teams statuses of my team—you know, the little green, yellow, or red dots—and I'd start seeing patterns. Like, if three of my senior devs went to 'Away' at the exact same minute, I'd become convinced it was a coordinated signal, a warning that they were meeting offline to discuss my performance or plan a walkout. I knew I wasn't manic, I wasn't pacing the floors, but the belief was just as strong. I'd sit there staring at the screen, refreshing the participant list, totally consumed by this idea that the statuses were a coded message meant specifically for me to decipher.

And the voices, too. Even when I was feeling totally level, just sitting in my office—not the server room, just my quiet office with the door closed—I'd hear these brief, passing comments. Just a quick, "He's missing it," or "Not good enough," right over my shoulder. I'd spin around in my chair, and obviously, no one was there. The office was empty. But I heard it clear as day. It didn't happen constantly like it did when I was in the server room during a high-energy phase, but it still happened enough to make me question my sanity even when I felt completely stable in every other way. It's like that part of my brain just... stays switched on, even when the rest of the system has powered down to normal operating levels. It's incredibly distracting, to be honest, trying to run a department when you're second-guessing whether the background noise is actually background noise or someone whispering about you.

During those times when your mood was completely level and you were experiencing the whispering voices or the coded message beliefs, how long did that stretch last in total—did it go on for two weeks or more before your mood shifted again?

Well, if I really sit down and think about the exact timeline—and I do think about it a lot, because as a systems guy, I'm always trying to find the root cause, right? I try to map out the variables and find the pattern. So, to answer your question, yes, absolutely, it was definitely two weeks, and honestly, usually longer than that. 

There have been several of these calm, or I guess you'd call them flat stretches, that went on for a few weeks at a time. And the strange part, the part that really throws a wrench in my whole logical understanding of what's happening to my brain, is that during those weeks, I wasn’t especially up, like I wasn't buzzing with that intense energy or skipping sleep, and I wasn't depressed or bogged down in that heavy gray zone either. I was just... normal. Waking up, commuting, getting my coffee, sitting at my desk, feeling completely baseline. 

But for those entire few weeks, day in and day out, I still fully believed that those Teams statuses were coded warnings. I would sit there, completely level-headed in every other respect, doing my regular tasks, but I'd be watching those little green and yellow dots, absolutely certain they were a coordinated signal about me. And the same goes for the auditory stuff. During those exact same multi-week stretches of totally normal mood, I still heard those brief comments when no one was there. I'd be completely alone in my office, feeling totally fine, and I'd hear someone whisper over my shoulder. So it wasn't just a day or two of carryover from a high-energy phase, it was a sustained period, literally weeks at a time, where my mood was completely stable, but the coded messages and the voices just kept right on going.

I’ll sit on the couch for hours, not really watching TV, not really reading, just existing in this gray zone where I have zero motivation and zero interest in anything that normally brings me joy. It’s the exact opposite of the high-energy phases, and honestly, it’s terrifying because when I’m in it, I can’t remember what it feels like to be happy or driven. I just feel broken.

inference.note: Confirmed presence of distinct depressive episodes with anhedonia, psychomotor slowing, and guilt, meeting criteria for a mood disorder with both manic and depressive phases, ruling out isolated manic episode (F30.1). No evidence of substance use or medical cause, ruling out F06.30. This supports a bipolar disorder diagnosis (F31.1/F31.9) rather than unipolar mania or organic mood disorder.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the high-energy episodes have ever caused severe impairment (e.g., needing hospitalization, causing job loss, reckless spending, or psychotic features) versus just being noticeable but manageable, to confirm if the episode meets full manic criteria rather than hypomania.
doctor.question: During your most intense high-energy periods, has it ever gotten so extreme that you were hospitalized, lost a job, made major financial decisions you regretted, or experienced things like hearing or seeing things that weren't there?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: During my most driven stretches, when I was barely sleeping and pushing huge plans, I was also hearing comments in the server noise and reading hidden threats into work messages.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if during the high-energy periods the patient experienced severe consequences or psychotic symptoms (hearing/seeing things). This maps perfectly to the concurrent occurrence of manic episodes and psychotic symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, I've never been hospitalized, and I still have my job, thankfully, though I've definitely had some close calls with HR because of how intense I can get during those stretches. And I haven't gone out and bought a sports car or drained our savings account or anything like that. But... well, things did get really, really strange, and I guess extreme in a different way. 

It was during one of those most driven stretches, you know? When I was barely sleeping, maybe two hours a night, and I was pushing these huge, massive plans to restructure our entire cloud architecture. I was in the server room a lot, which is this incredibly loud, humming environment, right? It's just constant, white noise from the cooling fans. But I started... I started hearing things in the noise. Not just the hum, but actual voices, like comments being made about me. It sounded like people whispering just under the frequency of the fans, critiquing my work, saying I was missing something, or that I was being watched by corporate. I'd stop and hold my breath to listen, and it would fade back into just the fan noise, but the second I started working again, the whispering would start up. 

And then it bled over into my emails and Slack messages. I'd be reading a totally standard message from a vendor or a colleague—something like, "Let's review the deployment schedule on Tuesday"—and I would read these hidden threats into it. I was convinced they were speaking in code, that "Tuesday" was a signal that they were going to try and force me out of my position, or that they had found a flaw in my code and were secretly building a case against me. I'd spend hours, literally hours, analyzing the phrasing of a three-word email, trying to decode the real message. I even started confronting people about it, very cryptically, which is why HR got involved. So, no hospital, no bankruptcy, but... yeah, my mind was definitely playing some terrifying tricks on me, making me see and hear things that, looking back, I know weren't really there. But in the moment, I swear to you, it felt as real as you sitting across from me right now.

inference.note: Patient endorsed clear psychotic features (auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusions) occurring specifically during the high-energy/manic periods, confirming a manic episode with psychotic features rather than without. This rules out F31.1 (severe manic without psychotic features) and F31.9 (unspecified), narrowing the diagnosis to Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic, severe with psychotic features.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms (hearing voices, paranoid interpretations) occur only during the high-energy manic periods, or if they also happen during the depressive episodes or when his mood is otherwise normal
doctor.question: Have you ever experienced that whispering or hearing hidden messages in emails during your low, depressed periods or when you're feeling like your normal self, or does it only happen during those high-energy stretches?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There have been several calm or flat stretches, including a few weeks at a time, when I wasn’t especially up or depressed but still believed Teams statuses were coded warnings and still heard brief comments when no one was there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the psychotic symptoms (hearing whispers, seeing hidden messages) occur during periods when I am not in a high-energy or depressed state (i.e., in the absence of a major mood episode).

patient.answer:
Well, that's the thing, and it's something I've spent a lot of time trying to map out in my own head, because you'd think it would just be tied to the lack of sleep and the overdrive, right? Like, the brain is just misfiring from running too hot. But... no, it's not just then. 

I've had periods—several of them, actually—where my mood was completely flat. Not depressed, not lying in bed unable to move, but not energized either. Just... normal, I guess? Or as close to normal as I get. Just calm, going through the motions, sleeping eight hours, eating regular meals. And even during those stretches, which have lasted a few weeks at a time, I've still experienced it. 

I remember one specific time, it was maybe a month after HR talked to me, and I was really making an effort to just lay low and do my job. I felt fine. But I'd look at the Microsoft Teams statuses of my team—you know, the little green, yellow, or red dots—and I'd start seeing patterns. Like, if three of my senior devs went to 'Away' at the exact same minute, I'd become convinced it was a coordinated signal, a warning that they were meeting offline to discuss my performance or plan a walkout. I knew I wasn't manic, I wasn't pacing the floors, but the belief was just as strong. I'd sit there staring at the screen, refreshing the participant list, totally consumed by this idea that the statuses were a coded message meant specifically for me to decipher.

And the voices, too. Even when I was feeling totally level, just sitting in my office—not the server room, just my quiet office with the door closed—I'd hear these brief, passing comments. Just a quick, "He's missing it," or "Not good enough," right over my shoulder. I'd spin around in my chair, and obviously, no one was there. The office was empty. But I heard it clear as day. It didn't happen constantly like it did when I was in the server room during a high-energy phase, but it still happened enough to make me question my sanity even when I felt completely stable in every other way. It's like that part of my brain just... stays switched on, even when the rest of the system has powered down to normal operating levels. It's incredibly distracting, to be honest, trying to run a department when you're second-guessing whether the background noise is actually background noise or someone whispering about you.

inference.note: Patient reports psychotic symptoms (whispered voices, delusional interpretation of Teams statuses) persisting during euthymic periods lasting weeks, not confined to manic or depressive episodes. This raises strong suspicion for schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type (F25.0), since psychotic symptoms outside mood episodes for a substantial duration is a key differentiator from bipolar disorder with psychotic features (F31.2).

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms (voices, coded messages) have occurred for at least 2 continuous weeks without any accompanying mood episode (manic or depressive), which is required to distinguish schizoaffective disorder from a mood disorder with psychotic features
doctor.question: During those times when your mood was completely level and you were experiencing the whispering voices or the coded message beliefs, how long did that stretch last in total—did it go on for two weeks or more before your mood shifted again?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There have been several calm or flat stretches, including a few weeks at a time, when I wasn’t especially up or depressed but still believed Teams statuses were coded warnings and still heard brief comments when no one was there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the psychotic symptoms (whispering voices, coded messages) during periods of normal mood, specifically checking if it lasted for 2 weeks or more. This directly corresponds to Additional Requirement 3.

patient.answer:
Well, if I really sit down and think about the exact timeline—and I do think about it a lot, because as a systems guy, I'm always trying to find the root cause, right? I try to map out the variables and find the pattern. So, to answer your question, yes, absolutely, it was definitely two weeks, and honestly, usually longer than that. 

There have been several of these calm, or I guess you'd call them flat stretches, that went on for a few weeks at a time. And the strange part, the part that really throws a wrench in my whole logical understanding of what's happening to my brain, is that during those weeks, I wasn’t especially up, like I wasn't buzzing with that intense energy or skipping sleep, and I wasn't depressed or bogged down in that heavy gray zone either. I was just... normal. Waking up, commuting, getting my coffee, sitting at my desk, feeling completely baseline. 

But for those entire few weeks, day in and day out, I still fully believed that those Teams statuses were coded warnings. I would sit there, completely level-headed in every other respect, doing my regular tasks, but I'd be watching those little green and yellow dots, absolutely certain they were a coordinated signal about me. And the same goes for the auditory stuff. During those exact same multi-week stretches of totally normal mood, I still heard those brief comments when no one was there. I'd be completely alone in my office, feeling totally fine, and I'd hear someone whisper over my shoulder. So it wasn't just a day or two of carryover from a high-energy phase, it was a sustained period, literally weeks at a time, where my mood was completely stable, but the coded messages and the voices just kept right on going.

inference.note: Patient confirms psychotic symptoms (whispered voices, delusional beliefs about coded messages) persisted for multiple weeks during periods of clearly euthymic, stable mood—not just during manic or depressive episodes. This rules out F31.2 (bipolar disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features only during episodes), since ICD-10 criteria for bipolar with psychotic features require psychosis to be confined to the mood episode. The sustained psychosis independent of mood state supports schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type.
